pages.title: The deal is decided before the deal
pages.caption: the résumé comes with the tool
pages.body:
Three pieces went out this month, and they kept arriving at the same place.

Clay grew by giving a job title to its best users. By the time a company hires a GTM engineer, the person it hires already knows Clay. **The champion is inside the account before anyone signs.**

Datadog never asked a customer to rip anything out on day one. It plugged into what teams already ran and became the first place they looked when something broke.

The essay on framing makes the same point from the buyer’s side. In 6sense’s 2024 survey, 81% of buyers already had a preferred vendor when they first made contact.

None of these companies won the evaluation. **They won the part before it.**

pages.tocText: How a job title became a sales channel
pages.dek: The product, pricing, and community choices that made Clay the tool a new career is built on.

pages.pull: Software companies usually pay to train their customers. Clay was paying to train a job title.
pages.body:
On September 9, 2026, Clay announced a $115 million round at a $7.1 billion valuation. In the same announcement, it said it was putting $1 million into a scholarship fund to train GTM engineers.

The title had taken off. By early 2026 there were about 3,000 open GTM engineer roles across the major job boards, according to two separate industry analyses. One of them, the State of GTM Engineering Report, analyzed 3,342 postings and found that 69% mentioned Clay by name.

Four and a half years earlier, almost nobody wanted what Clay was selling. As of spring 2022 its revenue was “close to $0,” co-founder and CEO Kareem Amin told First Round Review. By December 2025, Clay said it had crossed $100 million in annual recurring revenue.

**What Clay did was find the people who already did growth work by hand, make them visibly better at it, and give them a name. Then it sold to the companies that hired them.**

pages.tocText: Why the company that frames the problem wins the deal
pages.title: Why the Company That Frames the Problem Wins the Deal
pages.body:
A deal can start slipping away before the buyer compares a single product.

By the time vendors enter the conversation, most buyers have already settled on an explanation for what’s wrong. A team frustrated with slow reporting decides it needs automation, without ever checking why the reports take so long to prepare.

That explanation shapes the competition. Once reporting speed is the priority, automation features and hours saved become the obvious scorecard.

In 6sense’s 2024 survey of more than 2,500 B2B buyers, 81% already had a preferred vendor when they first made contact.

**How a buyer explains the problem decides what they shop for. Shape the explanation and you shape the deal.**

pages.tocText: The company too valuable to sell
pages.dek: The pricing, product, and sales choices that made Datadog too valuable to sell.

pages.pull: It got onto every server, became the first place everyone looked when something broke, and sold them what they found there.
pages.body:
On September 18, 2019, Datadog priced its IPO at $27 a share. The next morning the stock opened at $40.35. By the close, the New York monitoring company was worth about $10.9 billion, according to Forbes.

It almost went another way. Weeks earlier, Bloomberg reported, Cisco had approached Datadog with a takeover offer “significantly higher” than the $7 billion valuation it was aiming for. Datadog said no.

Nine years earlier, almost nobody wanted Datadog at any price. “None of the West Coast investors were listening,” co-founder and CEO Olivier Pomel told TechCrunch.

The cloud is the obvious explanation, and it explains a lot. It doesn’t explain why the startups that rode the same wave sold for tens of millions while Datadog turned down billions.

pages.tocText: Three things to do before the next campaign
pages.title: CMO,
Letter to the CMO
pages.body:
You don’t need a new campaign this month. You need a look at the part of the deal you never see.

**Read five lost deals backwards.** Put the buyer’s first requirements next to their final objections. If the brief was written before you arrived, find out who wrote it.

**Find your hand-builders.** Somewhere in your customer base, people are already doing your product’s job with spreadsheets and workarounds. Clay found its market in thirty interviews. Ask what would make those people look good in public.

**Make the first yes small.** Datadog’s first sale didn’t ask anyone to replace anything. A purchase that adds to what a team already runs is easier to approve than one that replaces it.

None of this shows up in a dashboard yet. By the time it does, the frame is already set.
